Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.

abstract.label: MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS
abstract.text: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

articles.title: Current models of emergency general surgery care delivery in Manitoba, Canada: a cross-sectional survey.
articles.journal_full: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency general surgery conditions result in disproportionately high rates of morbidity and mortality. Despite this, little is known about the resources available for related care in Canadian hospitals. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures dedicated to emergency general surgery in Manitoba, Canada.

abstract.label: METHODOLOGY
abstract.text: We developed a survey to examine institutional capabilities in providing emergency general surgical care. The survey was developed over three iterations using a modified Delphi technique and was then reviewed separately by community surgeons to ensure broad applicability. A cross-sectional survey of representatives at each of the fourteen hospitals reported to offer emergency general surgery care in Manitoba was performed in two iterations between March and December 2023. Findings were examined descriptively and stratified between tertiary, urban, and rural centres. Our aim was to describe the resources and structures in place for providing related care, including the proportion of hospitals with a dedicated emergency general surgery care model.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: After exclusions and non-responses, we examined the resources and capabilities of nine institutions. Two tertiary, two urban community, and five rural community centres were evaluated. Of these institutions, 4/9 (44.4%) had an emergency general surgery model of care, including one rural centre. There was a large degree of variation in operative resources, specialty services, and physician learners between centre types. Allied health professionals were more consistently available across hospitals. Our survey results identified several pertinent gaps in care, including a lack of shared treatment protocols, transfer agreements, and quality improvement measures, even at large tertiary centres.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This study demonstrates a pressing need for collaboration between centres and involvement in quality improvement amongst practitioners to meet standards of care in emergency general surgery. The results also show that important aspects of emergency general surgical care can be quantified with our survey and will serve as the basis for expanding this to a country-wide study.

articles.title: When emergency medicine isn't there: a scoping review of global acute care substitutes and complements for disaster response and surge capacity.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Disasters and everyday gaps in emergency care force acute illness and injury to be managed outside of formal emergency medicine (EM) and emergency medical services (EMS) systems. Because EM capacity varies substantially worldwide, this scoping review applies a substitutes-and-complements framework to the mechanisms that deliver acute care in and around formal EM or EMS, classifying their roles as substitutes, complements, or both across levels of EM system maturity and disaster conditions. The resulting typology serves as an inventory of latent disaster surge capacity.

abstract.label: MAIN TEXT
abstract.text: Following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, five databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and CINAHL) were searched, yielding 11,161 records. After title and abstract screening, 758 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility and 115 studies were included. We charted study type, country, and EM system maturity, using a codebook derived from American College of Emergency Physicians' (ACEP) International Ambassador country reports, the primary acute-care mechanism, care-delivery context, and COVID-19 relevance. Mechanisms were then classified by whether they substituted for or complemented formal EM. Publications were concentrated in the COVID-19 era (82/115, 71% from 2020 or later) and in high-income, mature-EM settings (United States 30%; 64/115 mature-EM). The most common mechanisms were lay and community first-responder programs (n = 18), hospital-at-home and remote monitoring (n = 15), and telehealth-based emergency and behavioral-health services. Overall, substitutes predominated (75/115), whereas complements (18/115) clustered in mature-EM systems.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Our inventory of latent surge capacity reframes each mechanism as a potential candidate for transfer across the EM-maturity spectrum: routine substitutes used in low-maturity systems may offer pre-planned crisis capacity for mature systems, while lower-infrastructure telehealth models may provide decision support or partial substitution where formal EM is limited. The substitute-complement balance tracks maturity, but the opportunity lies in translating mechanisms to the settings where they are not currently used as such.

articles.title: [New sepsis guidelines: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 and German Sepsis Society 2025 -Competing or complementary?].

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Sepsis is one of the leading causes of death in intensive care units worldwide. In German-speaking countries, patient management is primarily guided by two sets of guidelines: the international Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines and the S3 guidelines of the German Sepsis Society (DSG). While the DSG guidelines were published in 2025 as an evidence-based adaptation of the SSC 2021 guidelines, the SSC has since released an updated international version in 2026.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To provide a structured analysis of the key content areas, similarities and differences between the two guidelines, with a particular focus on the timing of treatment initiation, anti-infective treatment and hemodynamic management.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Both guidelines reflect not so much a fundamental shift in strategy but more a consolidation of evidence and a refinement of concepts. Three overarching themes can be identified: a broadened perspective encompassing the entire continuum of care, from the prehospital setting to post-sepsis follow-up, the increasing integration of antibiotic stewardship principles and in SSC 2026, the introduction of a graded sepsis terminology (definite/probable/possible/unlikely). Areas of agreement include the importance of early anti-infective treatment, the preferential use of balanced crystalloids, norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, the inclusion of capillary refill time as a perfusion parameter and a strong recommendation for prolonged or continuous beta-lactam infusion. Differences are evident in the specificity of antimicrobial recommendations, the definition of risk factors warranting empirical antifungal treatment and several new recommendations introduced in SSC 2026, such as a lower mean arterial pressure (MAP) target of 60-65 mm Hg for patients aged ≥ 65 years, initiation of treatment in the prehospital setting and source control within 6 h.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The DSG 2025 and SSC 2026 guidelines should be regarded as complementary rather than competing frameworks. The DSG 2025 remains the practical, high-resolution handbook for care in the Central European context, while the SSC 2026 outlines the international direction: away from a purely acute care set of rules towards an individualized, continuum-based model of care.

articles.title: Validation of the SPiRO Score for the Prediction of ICU Admission in Patients Presenting With Leptospirosis in Tropical Australia.
articles.journal_full: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: In some resource-limited settings the case-fatality rate of severe leptospirosis can exceed 50%. Early recognition of severe disease can expedite transfer to referral centres for advanced supportive care. The entirely clinical, 3-point SPiRO score can be calculated rapidly at presentation to predict a patient's subsequent clinical course. In its derivation study, a SPiRO score of 0 had a negative predictive value (NPV) for intensive care unit (ICU) admission of 98% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 96-99). In this validation cohort we sought to confirm the SPiRO score's prognostic utility and to compare its performance to other leptospirosis-specific and general disease severity scores.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We examined consecutive adults presenting to four high-caseload hospitals in tropical Australia with laboratory-confirmed leptospirosis between June 2016 and April 2026. The SPiRO score's ability to predict ICU admission before hospital discharge was compared with that of the leptospirosis-specific QuickLepto score and commonly used disease severity scores, namely the SOFA, qSOFA, qSOFA-lactate, NEWS-2, qNEWS, UVA and the SIRS scores.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: There were no deaths in 309 episodes of leptospirosis, but in 62 (20%) there was an ICU admission. The SPiRO score performed as well as, or better than, all the other scores in predicting ICU admission. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for the SPiRO score was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89); only the SOFA score had a higher value: 0.84 (0.79-0.90), although the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.08). The SPiRO score had the highest NPV for ICU admission of any of the scores: 95 (95% CI: 91-97)%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The SPiRO score can be calculated easily at the bedside at presentation to expedite the recognition of patients with leptospirosis who are most likely to deteriorate. In resource-limited settings this entirely clinical score can also help reduce unnecessary escalation of care, optimising the use of finite health resources.

articles.title: Experiences and perspectives of patients visiting Dutch emergency departments on opioid (mis)use: a qualitative interview study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND AND IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: The increase in opioid prescribing and opioid-related harm is a public health concern in many Western countries. Physicians in the emergency department (ED) frequently prescribe opioids for acute pain and play a role in the acute management of opioid-related harm. Yet, patient perspectives on the role of the ED in opioid management remain largely unexplored.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to explore how patients discharged from Dutch EDs with a new opioid prescription perceive ED opioid prescribing, the information and guidance they receive and the potential for opioid-related harm to inform safer opioid management in the ED.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: A qualitative interview study using semi-structured interviews.

abstract.label: SETTINGS AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: The study was conducted at two EDs in the Netherlands: Leiden University Medical Center (academic hospital) and Haaglanden Medical Center (teaching hospital). Adult patients (≥18 years) discharged from the ED with a new opioid prescription were recruited through purposive sampling. Patients (n=35) were interviewed either by telephone after discharge (n=28) or in person at the ED directly after discharge (n=7).

abstract.label: OUTCOME MEASURES AND ANALYSIS
abstract.text: Thematic analysis was performed to develop key themes reflecting patients' experiences and perspectives towards opioid use and potential misuse, in relation to an ED visit.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Three themes were developed from 35 interviews, encompassing: (1) Opioid prescribing practices at the ED; where patients described variable prescribing behaviours, limited information and lack of structured follow-up, (2) Navigating pain and dilemmas in opioid use; reflecting how acute pain drove opioid use despite concerns about side effects and stigma, (3) The perceived risk of opioid addiction after an ED visit; where patients acknowledged risks but often considered themselves protected by resilience, self-regulation and social support.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These findings show that while ED patients trust physicians’ prescribing, insufficient communication and aftercare leave them uncertain about safe opioid use and tapering. Implementing standardised, patient-centred discharge instructions and follow-up could strengthen safe opioid-prescribing practices at the ED, support patients in managing acute pain and may help to reduce the risk of long-term opioid-related harm.

articles.title: Reciprocity between the intestinal microbiome and urobiome in children with and without urinary tract infection: protocol of a single-centre, nested case-control study in Denmark.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is a common paediatric infection, usually caused by bacteria originating from the child’s own gastrointestinal tract. The underlying dynamics of the intestinal microbiome and urobiome in the development of UTI remains poorly understood. We aim to characterise and compare microbial diversity and composition in stool and urine samples from children suspected of UTI to identify potential bacterial compositions which are associated with the development of UTI.

abstract.label: METHODS AND ANALYSES
abstract.text: In this nested case–control study, paired stool and urine samples will be collected from 100 children up to 7 years of age undergoing clinical evaluation for suspected UTI at the paediatric emergency department at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre. Participants will be stratified depending on confirmed UTI status (UTI vs non-UTI group). Parents will answer a questionnaire on gastrointestinal symptoms, antibiotic use and other relevant exposures. Urine samples will be cultured and analysed at the Department of Clinical Microbiology, Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre, as part of the routine clinical evaluation. Microbiome analyses of stool and urine samples will be performed at the Department of Science and Environment, Roskilde University, using expanded quantitative culturing, 16s rRNA gene sequencing (V4 region) and proteomics analyses. Subsequent bioinformatic analyses will be performed using QIIME2 and PICRUSt2. Co-primary outcomes are alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance of the intestinal microbiome and urobiome between groups. Secondary outcomes are associations between selected exposures and UTI risk, assessed using logistic regression models.

abstract.label: ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
abstract.text: The study is part of the CHILD project conducted in the Capital Region of Denmark. This study has been approved by the Committees on Health Research Ethics in the Capital Region of Denmark (H-18065635) and the Danish Data Protection Agency (P-2025-19963). Oral and written consent will be obtained from parent(s) or legal guardian(s) of eligible children before inclusion. Regardless of the study’s findings (whether conclusive or inconclusive), the results will be compiled into one or more manuscripts for publication in international peer-reviewed scientific journals and presented at conferences.

abstract.label: STUDY REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Not applicable, as this is an observational study in which no intervention is assigned.

articles.title: Characteristics, Implementation and Effects of Nurse-Driven Sepsis Protocols in Hospital Settings: A Systematic Review.

abstract.label: AIMS
abstract.text: To synthesize evidence on the characteristics, implementation and effects of nurse-driven sepsis protocols on process-of-care indicators and clinical outcomes.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Systematic review without meta-analysis.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Studies were included if they described and evaluated nurse-driven sepsis protocols in hospitals. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts for eligibility. The Johns Hopkins Nursing Evidence-Based Practice model was used to appraise included studies. Data were extracted and narratively synthesized.

abstract.label: DATA SOURCES
abstract.text: Eight databases were searched from database inception to 30 June 2025.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Fifteen studies were included, most using before-and-after designs and conducted in the emergency departments (n = 7) and hospital-wide settings (n = 4). Protocols commonly used systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria for screening (n = 12) and incorporated key Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendations (n = 14). Most studies reported improved or comparable outcomes to baseline in overall sepsis bundle compliance and key process-of-care indicators, including timely antibiotic administration, blood culture collection, lactate measurement and fluid administration. All 11 studies evaluating mortality reported reductions, although only four were statistically significant. Findings for hospital length of stay were inconsistent. Common implementation strategies included nurse education and training, coupled with audit and feedback.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Nurse-driven sepsis protocols may improve adherence to and timeliness of key sepsis care processes. Effects on clinical outcomes are less certain, given the predominance of before-and-after designs and inconsistent findings for hospital length of stay. The review identifies implementation strategies that can guide future sepsis quality improvement initiatives.

abstract.label: IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE
abstract.text: Nurse-driven protocols may support nurses in initiating timely sepsis care and strengthening adherence to recommended care processes. Further high-quality studies are needed to establish effects on clinical outcomes and broader impacts, including healthcare costs, intensive care resource utilization, patient and nurse satisfaction, and safety outcomes.

abstract.label: PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION
abstract.text: No patient or public contribution.

articles.title: Design of a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial: Reducing high risk polypharmacy using behavioral economics through electronic health records.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Inappropriate polypharmacy can lead to harms among older adults. Behavioral nudges delivered using decision support in electronic health records (EHR) may be a scalable way to reduce polypharmacy. The goal of the High-Risk PolyPharmacy (HRPP) trial is to evaluate the effectiveness of a 'commitment nudge' and a 'justification nudge' alone and in combination on reducing HRPP via a pragmatic, clinic-randomized trial among patients aged 65 years and older.

abstract.label: METHODS/DESIGN
abstract.text: This 2 × 2 clinic-randomized factorial trial in primary care clinics in two health systems has four parallel arms: EHR commitment nudge, EHR justification nudge, both, or neither, all coupled with optional clinician education activities. Eligible patients are aged ≥65 years actively using ≥5 systemic, oral medications. The primary outcome is a composite of seven indicators of HRPP. Secondary outcomes include the individual components of HRPP and measures of health system burden: all-cause and adverse drug event-specific emergency department (ED) visits and ED visits followed by hospitalization.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We used constrained randomization to produce balance between study arms for 124 primary care clinics comprising 804 clinicians. At randomization, the median (range) practice had 573 (326-947) eligible patients; the average clinic-level prevalence of HRPP among these patients was 30.0%. The 18-month intervention began in 2023-October and 2024-November at NM and UPMC, respectively. Data collection will end in 2026-April at NM and 2026-December at UPMC.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: This trial is evaluating the effectiveness and safety of EHR-embedded interventions to reduce HRPP. If successful, this intervention could offer a low-cost, scalable solution.

articles.title: Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: a systematic review.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with survival strongly dependent on rapid recognition and timely emergency care. Wearables capable of automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting may reduce delays to treatment, particularly in unwitnessed arrests. Therefore, this review aims to systematically evaluate the existing evidence on the performance of wearable sensors and algorithms designed for OHCA detection.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A systematic search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Libraries, forward citation and backward citation to identify all eligible studies up to 22 September 2026. Studies describing non-invasive, intended wearable systems designed to detect OHCA and reporting on their detection performance were included. The methodology and report of the present review are based on recommendations of the PRISMA statement and Cochrane Collaboration. Primary outcome is the sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection. Secondary outcomes include false positives cardiac arrest alerts and specificity. Studies were evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: From 6,344 records screened, 13 publications were included with the number of participants ranging from 18 to 1,423. Wristbands were the most prevalent device type (n = 9). Nine studies used photoplethysmography as primary sensor type, with accelerometry as additive sensor modality (n = 2). Other sensors used were mechanical plethysmography (n = 1), electrocardiography (n = 1), sound-based (n = 1) and a nonlinear resonant circuit (n = 1). Sensitivity ranged between 43.8 and 100%, with ten studies reporting a sensitivity of ≥90%. False positives ranged between multiple per day and one per twenty-one user-years.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Wearable devices have demonstrated promising sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest. However, (external) validation and real-life data are scarce, and the sensitivity-false alarm trade-off requires further investigation.

abstract.label: REGISTRATION
abstract.text: OSF, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AEPF8.

articles.title: Long-term survival following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a two-center five-year analysis.

abstract.text: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years and 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

articles.title: Post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation and coronary angiographic phenotypes in angiography-evaluable survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The clinical meaning of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with suspected coronary etiology remains uncertain. We aimed to describe coronary angiographic phenotypes and clinical outcomes according to post-resuscitation ST-segment findings in an angiography-evaluable subset of OHCA survivors with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We retrospectively analyzed 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients admitted to our institution between January 2015 and December 2023, who underwent post-resuscitation coronary angiography and had presumed culprit lesions, defined by integrating angiographic findings with electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and biomarker data in the clinical context. Patients were classified according to the presence or absence of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: ST-segment elevation was associated with a more acute occlusive coronary phenotype, with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury. In contrast, patients without ST-segment elevation more frequently had multivessel disease and chronic total occlusion, suggesting more complex coronary artery disease. Favorable neurological outcome was less frequent with ST-segment elevation in unadjusted analyses, but this association was not independent of pre-hospital factors.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this selected OHCA subset, post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation was associated with an acute occlusive coronary phenotype and greater myocardial injury, as in non-arrest acute coronary syndromes. However, the absence of ST-segment elevation did not exclude a coronary culprit lesion, so comprehensive coronary assessment is essential. ST-segment elevation was not independently associated with clinical outcomes after adjustment for pre-hospital factors. These findings should be interpreted considering substantial selection inherent to the study population.

articles.title: [Emergencies during heat-related extreme weather events].

abstract.text: Climate change is placing an increasing burden on emergency medical care. In addition to heat-related illnesses, exacerbations of common chronic diseases and a higher incidence of injuries are major contributors to the growing number of emergency department presentations. At the same time, vector-borne diseases and other climate-related health risks are becoming increasingly relevant. Against the backdrop of demographic change, strengthening societal resilience, improving public health literacy, and implementing effective heat protection measures are of particular importance. In addition to prevention and public education, regular review of heat-sensitive medications should be considered an essential component of patient care. Overall, the health consequences of climate change are emerging as a major challenge for both prehospital and hospital emergency care, underscoring the need for timely adaptation of healthcare systems and emergency care strategies.

articles.title: Mapping the evidence on implementation of clinical decision support systems in nurses' reverse triage decisions during disaster surges: A scoping review with a proposed conceptual framework.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Emergency and critical care nurses are increasingly required to make complex, time-sensitive decisions across intensive care unit (ICU), emergency department, prehospital, and telephone triage settings, and clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) have been proposed as a technological strategy to support this process. However, the extent to which CDSSs influence nurses' decision-making time, accuracy, and confidence remains uncertain-particularly for reverse triage during disaster surges, an area of growing importance for emergency nursing preparedness worldwide. No previous review has synthesised evidence at the intersection of CDSS technology and reverse triage. This scoping review aimed to map existing evidence on the implementation of CDSSs in nurses' decision-making across ICU and triage settings, and to identify evidence gaps concerning reverse triage during disaster surges, in order to propose a novel conceptual framework-the CDSS-RT (Clinical Decision Support System for Reverse Triage) framework.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A scoping review following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR was conducted and prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF registration: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/VKRHU). Systematic searches across MEDLINE, Scopus, CINAHL, Embase, and the Cochrane Library identified English-language studies published up to January 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. An evidence gap map was constructed to visualise literature distribution and gaps.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: From 4218 records, 22 studies met inclusion criteria, published between 2009 and 2026 across 13 countries. CDSSs were predominantly knowledge-based, with growing use of machine learning and artificial intelligence. CDSSs improved triage accuracy by 7-23 percentage points, reduced cognitive workload, and enhanced confidence, although alert fatigue, increased response time, and limited system integration were common barriers. The evidence gap map revealed a critical absence of studies addressing CDSSs in reverse triage during disaster surges.

abstract.label: PROPOSED CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
abstract.text: The CDSS-RT framework, grounded in the CDS Five Rights, CFIR, and Dual-Process Theory, integrates six components: (1) knowledge base; (2) hybrid reasoning engine; (3) user cognitive factors; (4) implementation readiness; (5) context-sensitive design; and (6) multi-level outcome metrics.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Conclusion and implications: CDSSs show considerable promise for nursing decision-making in ICU and triage settings relevant to emergency nursing practice internationally. The proposed CDSS-RT framework provides a structured foundation for future CDSS-assisted reverse triage research and system design.

articles.title: Pediatric emergency medicine in Lebanon: Physician-perceived comfort levels, challenges, and educational needs.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pediatric Emergency Medicine (PEM) is a rapidly evolving subspecialty that improves the quality and safety of care for children. Despite global advancements, PEM remains underdeveloped in many low- and middle-income countries, including Lebanon. Despite a large pediatric population there is no formal paediatric emergency medicine system in place, and care largely delivered by physicians practicing without standardized or specialized training. This lack of dedicated PEM training and organized emergency care pathways may compromise the timely recognition and management of pediatric emergencies, potentially affecting patient outcomes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: The present study aimed to assess physicians perceived comfort in managing pediatric emergencies, identify training gaps, and explore systemic and institutional challenges affecting pediatric emergency care in Lebanon.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted among physicians involved in pediatric emergency care across Lebanon. The questionnaire assessed self-reported comfort in managing pediatric emergencies, perceived challenges, and priorities for training and PEM workforce development.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Responses from 59 physicians were analysed. Most were male 38 (64.4%), with a median clinical experience of 7 years. General pediatricians represented 28 (47.5%), emergency physicians 17 (28.8%), PEM specialists 8 (13.6%), and pediatric intensivists 6 (10.2%). Physicians reported high perceived comfort in pediatric fluid management 52(88.1%), chest X-ray interpretation 46 (77.9%), and general pediatric emergencies 42 (71.2%), but lower comfort in procedural sedation, suturing 35 (59.6%), fracture stabilization 35 (59.4%), and Extended Focused Assessment Sonography in Trauma (EFAST) 22 (41.8%). General pediatricians reported greater comfort with general pediatric emergencies, while emergency-focused physicians had higher comfort with trauma-related skills and procedural interventions. Major challenges included gaps in practical and theoretical training, limited hospital infrastructure, shortages of devices and human resources, and the need for continuing medical education. Nearly all participants 57 (96.6%) supported the establishing a dedicated PEM fellowship, highlighting training priorities in trauma, medical emergencies, life support, procedural skills, and pediatric imaging.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Pediatric emergency care in Lebanon is constrained by gaps in skills, training, and systemic resources. There is an urgent need to establish standardized PEM training pathways, enhance curricula, and strengthen system-level preparedness. Implementing these measures will support a competent PEM workforce and improve the quality and safety of emergency care for children nationwide.

articles.title: Knowledge and experiences of overdose among formerly incarcerated people living with HIV and hazardous opioid use in South Africa: A qualitative study.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Drug overdose is a leading cause of death among people released from correctional facilities, and the risk of overdose is higher among people living with HIV (PLWH). Overdose remains understudied in people in South Africa despite the high burden of HIV and hazardous opioid use. The researchers aimed to qualitatively explore how formerly incarcerated people living with HIV and OUD in South Africa understand, experience, and respond to overdose.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: People with HIV and self-reported hazardous opioid use prior to correctional facility release or shortly after release were enrolled in a convenience sample. Twenty-three formerly incarcerated people living with HIV and opioid use in or around Tshwane, South Africa completed sequential in-depth interviews that explored medication-assisted treatment for hazardous opioid use and HIV care delivery. Transcripts were analyzed thematically using both deductive and inductive coding, with a focus on participants' knowledge and definition of overdose, personal experiences with overdose, and responses to overdose.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: All participants used the term "overdose", but there was no unified understanding of what constitutes an overdose or how to manage an overdose. The period immediately following release from incarceration was identified as a key moment in which overdose occurred. Pouring water onto the person overdosing was reported to be the most prevalent response strategy. Only two participants contacted or watched their peers contact the ambulance. Fear of law enforcement involvement was perceived as a barrier to calling for emergency services.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The findings identify a gap in overdose knowledge among corrections-involved people living with HIV and hazardous opioid use in South Africa. There is a need to increase knowledge regarding overdose recognition and responses.

articles.title: An Approach to Acute Cranial Symptoms in Primary Care: Lesson From a Case of Miller Fisher Syndrome.
articles.journal_full: The American journal of case reports

abstract.text: BACKGROUND Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) is a rare variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome characterized by the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia following a recent infection. Early recognition is particularly challenging due to the rarity of the condition and its tendency to mimic other common neurological and non-neurological disorders. We report a case highlighting the diagnostic and referral challenges encountered in the primary care setting. CASE REPORT A 38-year-old woman with no significant comorbidity presented to a primary care clinic with acute diplopia, right eye pain, headache, and perioral numbness following an upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks earlier. Initial neurological examination was unremarkable. She was referred to the ophthalmology and emergency departments to exclude ocular pathology and posterior circulation stroke. Laboratory investigation and computed tomography of the brain were unremarkable and she was managed as a case of migraine. Meanwhile, ophthalmological review subsequently demonstrated ophthalmoplegia and the following day she developed bulbar symptoms prompting urgent neurological consultation. Repeated neurological examination revealed the classic triad of MFS. She received plasma exchange therapy following her clinical deterioration. Her neurological symptoms gradually improved with complete recovery, with residual diplopia resolving 8 weeks after symptom onset. CONCLUSIONS MFS remains a predominantly clinical diagnosis with subtle and evolving features that may delay recognition in the primary care setting. This case underscores the crucial role of primary care physicians in maintaining a high index of suspicion, recognizing atypical presentation, and providing appropriate safety-netting and timely specialist referral to facilitate early diagnosis and improve clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Ninety-Day Overall Healthcare Reimbursements and Their Drivers for Primary Arthroscopic Bankart Repair.
articles.journal: J Am Acad Orthop Surg Glob Res Rev
articles.journal_full: Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons. Global research & reviews

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Arthroscopic Bankart repair (ABR) is a widely performed procedure for anterior glenohumeral instability. The aim of this study was to characterize variability and identify drivers of 90-day healthcare reimbursement after primary ABR.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Primary ABR patients were identified in the PearlDiver M170 database (January 2010-April 2023). Patients who were inactive within 90 days preoperatively or postoperatively or who were coded for neoplasm or infection within 90 days preoperatively were excluded. Variables analyzed included patient characteristics (age, sex, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index [ECI]), nonclinical factors (insurance plan, geographic region), postoperative events (any adverse event [AAE], emergency department [ED] visit, hospital readmission), and total 90-day reimbursements. Multivariable linear regression was conducted to identify independent predictors of reimbursement.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall, 135,144 primary ABR patients were identified, representing $596,112,149 in total reimbursements. The mean ± SD reimbursement was $4450 ± $5268. The median (25th quartile-75th quartile) reimbursement was $3192 ($1751-$5465).Variables independently associated with the greatest 90-day reimbursement were readmission (+$18060), AAE (+$1169), and ED visit ($1044). Weaker associations were observed for geographic region, ECI, and male sex (P < 0.0001 for all). Compared with commercial insurance, Medicare (-$2072) and Medicaid (-$1371) were associated with lower reimbursement (P < 0.0001 for both). Notably, over the course of the study period, median overall reimbursement increased from $1930 to $3540 (P < 0.0001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This longitudinal, national analysis identified cost variability and key drivers related to ABR. Preventing readmissions may yield the largest cost reductions while observed disparities across insurance plans and regions highlight opportunities for standardization and equity in reimbursement.

articles.title: Timing matters: Delayed surgery increases mortality for blunt hollow viscus injury.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Immediate surgical exploration is recommended for suspected hollow viscus injury (HVI) following blunt trauma. However, diagnostic uncertainty can lead to delayed operative management. We aimed to evaluate if delayed bowel resection/repair (DBR), defined as ≥8 hours after emergency department arrival, was independently associated with increased mortality in blunt trauma patients. We also sought to identify risk factors associated with DBR.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The Trauma Quality Improvement Program database (2017-2024) was queried for admitted adults with blunt abdominal trauma (abdomen abbreviated injury scale grade ≥2) who underwent bowel resection/repair. Patients who were transferred from another facility or died within 8 hours were excluded. Patients undergoing early bowel resection <8 hours (EBR) were compared with patients undergoing DBR (≥8 h). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between DBR and mortality, controlling for age, severe head and thoracic injury, intubation within 1 hour of arrival, injury to the small bowel, colon, or rectum, and blood transfusion within 4 hours.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 33,728 patients undergoing bowel resection/repair, 16,010 (47.5%) underwent DBR. The DBR cohort had lower rates of small bowel (49.6% vs. 53.9%, p<0.001) and colon (46.7% vs. 49.7%, p<0.001) injuries, but similar rates of rectal injury (4.4% vs. 4.1%, p=0.166). Injuries to the liver (26.8% vs. 20.8%), spleen (28.2% vs. 23.4%), and kidney (12.9% vs. 9.0%) were more frequent in the DBR cohort (all p<0.001). DBR patients had an increased associated risk of mortality (13.0% vs. 8.5%, OR 1.21, 95% CI: 1.12-1.30, p<0.001). Small bowel injury was the only independent factor with decreased associated risk of DBR (OR 0.93, CI: 0.89-0.97, p=0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Delayed operative management for blunt HVI occurs more often in patients with solid organ injuries and is independently associated with increased mortality. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and timely surgical management of HVI.

abstract.label: LEVEL OF EVIDENCE
abstract.text: Therapeutic/Care Management, Level IV.

articles.title: Defining the therapeutic window for ADAMTS13 modulation in early trauma-induced coagulopathy.
articles.journal_full: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

articles.title: Delirium and Long-Term Cognitive Trajectories in Cognitively Unimpaired Adults.

abstract.label: IMPORTANCE
abstract.text: Delirium is a state of acute confusion characterized by deficits in attention that occurs commonly during hospitalization and is associated with adverse outcomes; however, the association of delirium with longitudinal cognitive trajectories is not fully understood.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To evaluate the association of delirium during hospitalization with subsequent development of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), dementia, and longitudinal cognitive trajectories.

abstract.label: DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: This cohort study used data from participants with hospitalizations in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging (MCSA) from October 2004 to December 2023. The MCSA is a prospective, population-based longitudinal study of cognitive aging among residents of Olmsted County, Minnesota. Of participants enrolled in the MCSA between 2004 and 2023, individuals who experienced 1 or more hospitalization prior to their last MCSA encounter were included in this study. Participants with dementia at MCSA enrollment or prior to first hospitalization were excluded. Follow-up continued until development of MCI or dementia, last MCSA visit, or the end of the study.

abstract.label: EXPOSURE
abstract.text: Delirium was identified using a validated natural language processing algorithm applied to clinical notes from hospitalizations, associated emergency department visits, and follow-up within 30 days after hospitalization. Delirium status was modeled as a time-dependent exposure.

abstract.label: MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES
abstract.text: Incident MCI and dementia were assigned through MCSA expert consensus evaluations, including neuropsychological testing performed every 15 months. Association between delirium and development of MCI or dementia was assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusted for patient age, sex, level of education, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele carrier status; cognitive trajectories were assessed with linear mixed-effects models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 7030 participants enrolled in the MCSA, 3542 individuals experienced 1 or more hospitalization prior to their last MCSA encounter and were included, and 41 participants with dementia at enrollment or prior to first hospitalization were excluded. The cohort included 3501 participants with at least 1 hospitalization. Median (IQR) age was 74.1 (66.6-80.9) years, 1676 participants (47.9%) were female, median (IQR) level of education was 14 (12-16) years, and 910 participants (26.0%) were APOE ε4 carriers. During a median (IQR) follow-up of 7.2 (4.1-10.4) years, 75 participants (2.1%) had delirium documented within 30 days of hospitalization. Delirium was associated with increased risk of MCI (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 3.67; 95% CI, 2.19-6.15) and dementia (aHR, 5.39; 95% CI, 2.94-9.85) and with accelerated decline in longitudinal cognitive testing.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE
abstract.text: In this cohort study among adults in the MCSA, including those with unimpaired cognition at baseline, delirium during hospitalization was strongly associated with increased risk of MCI and dementia and accelerated cognitive decline in subsequent years.

articles.title: Use of hospital care among centenarians in France: implications for health-system planning in extreme old age-insights from a nationwide study of temporal patterns, regional variation and care settings (2014-2023).

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To describe nationwide hospital care use among centenarians in France, including temporal and regional variation, emergency admission, surgical care, and inpatient rehabilitation.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective nationwide observational study using French hospital discharge data on centenarian hospital stays from 2014 to 2023.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Over the study period, 110,585 acute care hospital stays were recorded among centenarians, of which 12.1% were surgical. Acute care hospitalization burden decreased from 53.2 stays per 100 centenarians in 2014 to 45.4 per 100 in 2023. Overall, 70.0% of acute care stays followed an emergency department admission, with this proportion increasing from 68.0% in 2014 to 72.9% in 2023. In-hospital mortality was 14.9% per stay; among fatal acute care stays, 9.4% ended in death on the day of admission. Marked regional variation was observed. Musculoskeletal conditions accounted for 16.9% of acute care stays and represented an increasing proportion over time. A total of 21,012 inpatient rehabilitation stays were recorded; rehabilitation hospitalization burden decreased from 10.3 to 8.3 stays per 100 centenarians, while the proportion related to musculoskeletal conditions increased.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: These descriptive nationwide findings may help inform health-system planning as the centenarian population continues to grow. Our results suggest that centenarians remain a clinically vulnerable population with substantial hospital care needs, requiring system-wide readiness beyond geriatric services. These findings may support more integrated care pathways, broader responses to falls and fractures, spanning prevention, acute care, and rehabilitation, and explicit consideration of the oldest-old in strategies addressing territorial and social inequalities in healthcare access.

articles.title: Refining ECPR candidate selection: from fixed criteria to a dynamic probability-of-benefit framework.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has emerged as a rescue strategy for selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest. However, identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically meaningful survival remains challenging. Conventional selection criteria, including age, initial rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and no-flow and low-flow duration, are clinically useful but may be insufficient when interpreted as isolated thresholds.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a narrative review of contemporary evidence on ECPR patient selection, incorporating randomized trials, observational studies, registries, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and current guideline and consensus recommendations. Evidence was critically evaluated with particular attention to patient-level prognostic factors, arrest setting, dynamic physiological and metabolic variables, ECPR logistics, and system-level determinants of outcome.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Current evidence supports a multidimensional rather than single-variable approach to ECPR candidacy. Favorable arrest characteristics, potentially reversible etiology, shorter low-flow duration, and preserved physiological reserve remain important; however, chronological low-flow time should be interpreted alongside the quality and effectiveness of ongoing CPR. Dynamic information-including transient return of spontaneous circulation, lactate kinetics, arterial pH, end-tidal carbon dioxide, and hemodynamic parameters-may further refine assessment of biological viability. Frailty, comorbidity burden, cerebral perfusion, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation-related contraindications should also be incorporated into decision-making. Importantly, selection cannot be separated from system performance: Cannulation strategy, transport logistics, institutional experience, and the ability to establish extracorporeal circulation rapidly may substantially modify the likelihood of benefit. Differences between out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest further limit the universal application of rigid eligibility criteria.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Candidacy for ECPR should be viewed as a dynamic, probability-based assessment rather than a checklist of fixed thresholds. Integrating arrest characteristics, reversibility, evolving physiology, patient reserve, and system capability may provide a more clinically meaningful framework for identifying patients most likely to achieve neurologically favorable survival after ECPR.

articles.title: The use of a non-invasive neuromonitoring device in the emergency department: comparison with computed tomography results.
articles.journal_full: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing

abstract.text: Computed tomography (CT) is widely used to evaluate emergency department (ED) patients with headache, increasing costs, radiation exposure, and workload. Non-invasive intracranial pressure waveform (ICPW) monitoring has been proposed as an adjunctive triage tool. We assessed its diagnostic performance for identifying abnormal head CT findings in ED patients with red-flag headaches and explored potential resource implications. This retrospective study included 84 patients with red-flag headaches at Hospital Leforte Morumbi, Brazil (June-September 2023). All underwent non-invasive ICPW monitoring (brain4care System) and head CT during the same ED encounter. ICPW was abnormal if P2/P1 ≥ 1.2 or time-to-peak (TTP) ≥ 0.3. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV, NPV) were calculated against abnormal CT. CT expenditure and ED length of stay were assessed as exploratory outcomes. ICPW showed 90.0% sensitivity, 66.2% specificity, 98.0% NPV, and 26.5% PPV for abnormal CT. Median P2/P1 ratio yielded an ROC AUC of 0.778 (95% CI 0.640-0.900). Forty-nine patients (58.3%) had both normal ICPW and normal CT; their median ED stay was 3.5 h shorter than that of the overall cohort, though causality cannot be inferred. One patient had normal ICPW despite abnormal CT. Hypothetically, the normal examinations represented a projected gross CT expenditure of US$34,300. The high NPV supports further investigation of ICPW as an adjunctive risk-stratification tool, but the retrospective single-center design, small sample, and few abnormal CTs preclude definitive conclusions. ICPW should not replace clinical assessment or neuroimaging; resource implications remain exploratory hypotheses requiring prospective, multicenter validation.

articles.title: Development and Validation of a Nomogram for Predicting Preoperative Venous Thromboembolism in Patients With Lower Extremity Fractures: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.journal_full: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis

abstract.text: BackgroundPatients with lower extremity fractures (LEF) are at high risk of preoperative venous thromboembolism (VTE). However, existing risk assessment models are not specifically developed and validated for this population.ObjectiveTo develop and validate a prediction model for preoperative VTE in emergency LEF patients, and to compare the performance of traditional logistic regression (LR) with that of machine learning (ML) algorithms.DesignRetrospective cohort study.SettingPeking University Shenzhen Hospital, China.Participants486 patients with LEF admitted between January 2022 and July 2025.MethodsTwo modeling strategies were compared: 1) a traditional LR nomogram using backward stepwise selection, and 2) nine ML algorithms with Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO)-based feature selection. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination (area under the curve, AUC), calibration, classification metrics (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity) and decision curve analysis.ResultsOf 486 enrolled patients, 79 (16.3%) developed preoperative VTE. Among the ML models, LASSO-LR and multilayer perceptron (MLP) achieved the highest validation AUCs (0.709 each), the best calibration and highest net benefit. The traditional LR nomogram showed an identical AUC of 0.709 (95% CI: 0.691-0.718), with superior calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.738, calibration intercept = -0.109, slope = 0.921) and better stability. Therefore, this simple five-predictor traditional LR nomogram, incorporating age ≥ 65 years, hemoglobin, glucose, external immobilization, and pre-injury anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, was selected as the optimal model.ConclusionThe traditional LR nomogram appears promising for preoperative VTE risk prediction in LEF patients. External validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Treatment of status epilepticus: Too low, too slow.

abstract.text: This review of the treatment of convulsive status epilepticus (SE) in adults examines why, with so many new tools, we have made so little progress. Major advances in basic mechanisms and increased number of available drugs, clinical trials, and publications have not led to a commensurate improvement in clinical outcomes. The central role of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in initiation and maintenance of SE is now understood, but its therapeutic implications have not been translated into clinical trials or clinical practice. Failure of inhibition from inactivation of synaptic γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors (GABAARs) and KCC2 chloride transporters and runaway excitation from increases in NMDA receptors (NMDARs) and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) are all under NMDAR control, yet no current guidelines recommend early treatment with NMDAR antagonists. Time plays a critical role in SE-associated morbidity and mortality, and in the response to benzodiazepines and antiseizure medications, yet most patients are treated after time t2 and are often underdosed. Traditional SE treatment leaves too much time for NMDAR-dependent pharmacoresistance to develop. There is a gap between the therapeutic strategies suggested by preclinical studies and the design of clinical trials, and between therapeutic recommendations from clinical trials and their real-life application (too low, too slow). Prehospital treatment should be standardized, home treatment should be encouraged, and underdosing is not acceptable. "Time-to-needle" must become an integral part of SE treatment. In untreated SE, if treatment delay (stage "1 plus") predicts failure of benzodiazepine monotherapy, more vigorous initial treatment should be considered. A recent double-blind pediatric SE study showed that initial treatment with midazolam plus ketamine was superior to and better tolerated than midazolam alone; we need a similar clinical trial in adults. When benzodiazepines fail, time to the next agent should be minimized, and we need a prehospital trial of ketamine as second agent. We have the tools to improve the outcome of SE; let us use them.

articles.title: Perioperative Single-Shot Regional Blocks and Associated Rebound Pain-Related Unscheduled Utilization of Health Care After Distal Radius Surgery.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Perioperative single-shot regional blocks are commonly used for pain control in outpatient distal radius fixation surgery. While regional blocks provide initial postoperative pain control, patients often experience significant rebound pain as the block effect dissipates, which can lead to utilization of unscheduled health care (emergency department visits, phone calls, and messages sent via the electronic health record [EHR] to providers). We hypothesized that patients who received perioperative blocks are more likely to use unscheduled health care versus those who did not.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A total of 619 patients underwent distal radius fracture fixation at a tertiary care academic center from 2013 to 2022. After excluding minors, inpatient and revision procedures, patients with insufficient records, and fixation of an impending pathologic fracture, 417 patients were included. Age, gender, mechanism, time to surgery, use of intraoperative local anesthetic, and whether a regional block was performed were collected. Returns to the emergency department, pain-related phone calls, and messages sent via the EHR system within 3 days of surgery were also collected.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The adjusted relative risk of using unscheduled health care for pain was 4.0 (95% CI, 1.3-12.1; P = .01) on postoperative day 1 for patients who received perioperative blocks compared with those who did not. Similarly, the adjusted relative risk within 2 days of surgery was 3.9 (95% CI, 1.4-10.5; P = .007) and within 3 days was 3.2 (95% CI, 1.4-7.5; P = .008).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Patients who receive perioperative regional blocks after distal radius fixation are more likely to use unscheduled health care within the first 3 days of surgery, compared with patients who did not receive blocks.

articles.title: Pain after endometriosis surgery: a retrospective cohort study.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Postoperative pain after endometriosis surgery has not been widely investigated, although these patients often present complex pain mechanisms. This study aimed to characterize postoperative pain and analgesic management in patients undergoing intra-abdominal endometriosis surgery at Skåne University Hospital Malmö (Sweden).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Background, surgical, anesthetic and intra- and postoperative data were collected from records of patients who underwent intra-abdominal endometriosis surgery between 2021 and 2025. The primary endpoint was the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) for pain at admission to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU). Secondary endpoints included NRS at PACU discharge, opioid use intraoperatively and in the PACU, and the need for pain therapy three weeks postoperatively. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used. Subgroup analyses compared pain in hysterectomy vs. other procedures and the analgesic effect of preemptive spinal analgesia in hysterectomy patients.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 155 patient's records were examined. More than half of patients reported an NRS>3 at PACU admission, median value 5 (IQ1-IQ3: 0-7). Median opioid consumption in the PACU was 9 (0-21) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME), while median intraoperative administration was 57 (14-90) OME mg. Fifty percent of the patients still required pain therapy three weeks after surgery and 14 % sought emergency care for abdominal pain not related to surgical complication within a month from discharge. Persistent pain at three weeks was associated with preoperative pain and the need for in-hospital pain service, but not with PACU NRS or opioid use. Hysterectomy patients required more opioids and longer PACU time, and preemptive spinal analgesia was associated with less need for pain therapy at three weeks after hysterectomy.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Persistent postoperative pain is common after endometriosis surgery. Preoperative pain history and the involvement of a pain specialist during admission predicted persistent pain at three weeks after surgery better than PACU pain intensity alone.

articles.title: Restrictive versus liberal red blood cell transfusion thresholds in haemodynamically stable adults: explaining variability in patient blood management guidelines.
articles.journal_full: Transfusion and apheresis science : official journal of the World Apheresis Association : official journal of the European Society for Haemapheresis

abstract.text: Patient Blood Management (PBM) promotes strategies to avoid unnecessary red blood cell transfusion. Guidelines broadly support restrictive transfusion for haemodynamically stable adults who are not actively bleeding, yet thresholds differ for some patient groups despite resting on the same trials. This narrative review examines landmark randomised trials (TRICC, FOCUS, TITRe2, REALITY, MINT, HEMOTION and TRAIN) and how they were incorporated into recommendations from major societies, including the 2025 AABB and ACC/AHA recommendations for acute myocardial infarction. For most stable adults, restrictive thresholds of 7-8 g/dL reduce transfusion exposure without increasing major adverse outcomes. Recommendations diverge where the certainty of evidence is lower. In acute myocardial infarction, MINT reported death or recurrent myocardial infarction at 30 days in 16.9% of restrictive-strategy and 14.5% of liberal-strategy patients (risk ratio 1.15; 95% CI 0.99-1.34); the 2025 AABB guideline conditionally recommends a liberal strategy (haemoglobin <10 g/dL) and the 2025 ACC/AHA guideline states that transfusion to maintain haemoglobin of at least 10 g/dL may be reasonable (Class 2b). In acute brain injury, HEMOTION and TRAIN reached different conclusions. These differences reflect populations, evidence certainty and guideline methodology rather than disagreement about PBM principles. We also consider why threshold trials so often show no difference, why haemoglobin is an imperfect surrogate for tissue oxygenation, and why thresholds do not apply to active haemorrhage. Prehospital whole blood showed no advantage over components, and the optimal timing of red cell transfusion in bleeding remains unresolved.

articles.title: Osteoporosis treatment gaps and risk of recurrent hip fracture following initial fragility fracture: Insights from over one million cases.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Patients who sustain a hip fracture are at high risk of a second hip fracture, yet most do not receive osteoporosis pharmacotherapy. We evaluated the association between bone-health medication initiation after a first hip fracture and the risk of a second hip fracture.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective cohort study used Epic Cosmos, a de-identified multi-institutional electronic health record database. Adults who underwent surgery for a first femoral neck, intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric hip fracture were classified as having no bone-health medication, as baseline users (medication documented at admission), or as initiators within six months of the index fracture. Second hip fracture was assessed over fixed 1-, 2- and 5-year horizons. We estimated absolute risks, cumulative incidence accounting for death as a competing risk, and multivariable cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Overall, 1,051,020 patients were eligible for the 5-year analysis: 705,059 (67.1%) had no medication, 83,452 (7.9%) were baseline users and 262,509 (25.0%) initiated medication within six months. Five-year cumulative incidence of second hip fracture was 17.2% (95% confidence interval [CI] 17.1-17.3) with no medication, 14.1% (95% CI 13.8-14.4) among baseline users and 8.9% (95% CI 8.8-9.1) among initiators. In adjusted models, the hazard of second hip fracture was lower among baseline users (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71, 95% CI 0.69-0.73) and initiators (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.37-0.39) than among patients with no medication.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Initiation of bone-health medication within six months of a first hip fracture was associated with a lower risk of a second hip fracture. Baseline users had intermediate risk, which may reflect confounding by indication, agent selection or adherence. These findings support early, coordinated post-fracture osteoporosis treatment; the observational design precludes causal inference.

articles.title: Articular compliance and tolerance to residual incongruity after intra-articular fracture: A hypothesis-driven narrative review.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Residual articular incongruity after intra-articular fracture is widely held to cause post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), yet tolerance of a given step-off differs between joints and between regions of the same joint. Reduction targets are nonetheless expressed as uniform millimetre thresholds, and no tissue-level mechanism has been offered for the variation.

abstract.label: HYPOTHESIS
abstract.text: The compliance of the osteochondral unit - cartilage thickness, cartilage material properties and subchondral bone stiffness together - modulates tolerance of residual incongruity, and incongruity is more informatively expressed relative to local cartilage thickness than in absolute millimetres.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Narrative review with a documented search of PubMed/MEDLINE (inception to 14 October 2026) covering cartilage and subchondral properties of opposing surfaces, experimental and computational studies of articular incongruity, and clinical studies relating residual displacement to outcome. Four searches returned 3928 records, 3579 after deduplication; 54 sources informed the synthesis. This is not a systematic review; reporting follows SANRA.

abstract.label: FINDINGS
abstract.text: Small, localised contact-stress elevations appear tolerable; step-offs remodel less completely as their height increases; and cumulative contact-stress exposure above a threshold predicts PTOA after tibial plafond fracture. Opposing surfaces differ measurably in cartilage thickness, modulus and subchondral bone thickness, but the direction of the difference reverses between joints and between regions of one joint, so curvature is not a usable proxy for compliance. Clinically, the acetabulum and tibial plafond appear least tolerant, the meniscus-covered tibial plateau more tolerant, and distal radius incongruity predicts radiographic arthrosis more strongly than functional loss.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The evidence is consistent with, but does not establish, a contribution of osteochondral compliance; joint-level factors confound the clinical data. We set out a Compliance Framework defining measurable determinants, propose relative incongruity as a testable metric, and state four falsifiable predictions with the designs that would test them. Current joint-specific reduction standards should guide practice until those predictions are tested.

articles.title: When Quality Indicators Become Competencies: Indonesia's New Emergency Medicine Standard and the Core Components of CBME.
Pedagogical Primer: Messick's Unified Validity Framework.

abstract.text: Medical training relies heavily on assessment. Although gathering validity evidence for assessments is critical, validity is often treated as a fixed property that a test either possesses or lacks. Building on earlier work by Cronbach and Meehl, Messick reshaped this model by proposing that validity belongs to the interpretation and uses of scores rather than to the instrument itself. He also challenged the traditional division of validity into separate types, proposing instead that content, criterion, and construct evidence represent complementary sources of evidence that together support a single, unified view of construct validity, in which theory connects a score to the construct it is meant to represent and the evidence supports a judgment about whether a score means what it is intended to mean. This Pedagogical Primer traces the origins of that view, the developments that followed, and how it now guides assessment in medical education and research. The framework was developed out of decades of debate in educational measurement and was later codified in the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, which describe five sources of validity evidence: content, response processes, internal structure, relationship to other variables, and the consequences of testing. Kane offered a complementary approach that lays out the chain of inferences within a validity argument, so that the evidence gathered matches the specific claims a score is being asked to support. The unified validity framework provides educators with a way to plan the evidence needed before using an assessment to make consequential decisions and gives researchers a standard for reporting validation work without overreaching conclusions. This framework requires significant and sustained effort. The amount of evidence needed should be proportional to the stakes of the decision, although there is no fixed rule for when sufficient evidence has been gathered. Despite this, Messick's unified validity framework remains a practical guide for building and defending the assessments on which training decisions rest.

articles.title: Learning Curve Cumulative Summation Method for Ocular Ultrasound.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The current American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) guidelines recommend that trainees perform 25 ocular ultrasound scans before being considered competent. This threshold has not been substantiated for ocular ultrasound. The purpose of this study was to determine the number of ocular scans required to reach competency in ocular ultrasound using the learning curve cumulative sum (LC-CUSUM) analysis. A secondary objective was to evaluate whether individualized learning curve feedback influences competency attainment.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Using the LC-CUSUM method with an 85% success threshold, we assessed the number of scans needed to achieve competency in both image acquisition and interpretation among first-year emergency medicine residents. For a secondary analysis, residents were then randomized into two groups: one receiving bimonthly personalized learning curve updates alongside standard feedback, and another receiving standard feedback alone. Competency attainment was compared between groups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-six residents were included. LC-CUSUM analysis determined that 21 studies were needed to reach competency. The median number of scans per resident was 26.5 (IQR: 22-30). At the end of the academic year, 17 residents (65%) reached technical competency, 10 residents (35%) reached interpretation competency, and 10 residents (35%) reached competency in both domains. Fifteen residents (58%) remained in the learning phase. There was no significant difference between competency attainment or perceived feedback in the randomized feedback groups.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: LC-CUSUM analysis suggests that competency in ocular ultrasound may be achieved after approximately 21 individual-eye scans, or approximately 10.5 bilateral ocular exams, fewer than half the 25 bilateral examinations recommended by ACEP. Individualized learning curve feedback did not improve competency attainment or perceptions of feedback compared with standard feedback.

articles.title: Comparative Analysis of Exonic SSR-Containing Genes in Three Diving Duck Species Reveals Shared Functional Themes.

abstract.text: Simple sequence repeats (SSRs) are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic genomes that contribute to genome evolution, genetic variation, and gene regulation. Although genome-wide SSR landscapes have been extensively characterized across vertebrates, the cross-species distribution and functional associations of exonic SSR-containing genes remain poorly understood, particularly in non-model birds. To address this knowledge gap, we performed a comparative analysis of chromosome-level genome assemblies from three diving duck species (Aythya ferina, Aythya marila, and Netta rufina) to investigate genome-wide SSR patterns and the cross-species sharing and functional characteristics of exonic SSR-containing genes. Comparative analyses of genome-wide SSRs revealed pronounced interspecific variation in SSR abundance and repeat composition, whereas exonic SSR abundance showed more similar values after normalization by total annotated exon sequence length. Cross-species comparison identified 4336 exonic SSR-containing genes shared among all three species, greatly outnumbering the species-specific gene sets. Functional enrichment analyses identified four broad functional themes associated with these shared genes: (i) gene transcription and epigenetic regulation, (ii) protein homeostasis and the ubiquitin-proteasome system, (iii) development, differentiation and morphogenesis, and (iv) stress response and cellular maintenance. The most significantly enriched categories were associated with transcriptional regulation, chromatin remodeling, RNA processing, and epigenetic regulation, whereas autophagy- and other cellular-maintenance pathways indicated additional associations with stress-response processes. These functional associations should be interpreted cautiously because they may be influenced by cross-species annotation limitations and gene-architecture differences. Collectively, our results reveal distinct patterns for genome-wide and exonic SSRs distribution among the three diving duck species and identify shared functional associations of genes containing exonic SSRs. These findings provide a comparative genomic framework for future investigations of exonic SSRs in waterfowl and other non-model vertebrates.

articles.title: Atypical Suprasyndesmotic Distal Fibular Fracture in an Adolescent Athlete with Minimal Symptoms: A Case Report.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Fractures of the distal fibula are common injuries in adolescent athletes, usually associated with identifiable trauma and rapid, uneventful healing. However, atypical mechanisms and minimal symptoms may obscure the diagnosis. We aim to describe the clinical course, imaging findings, and management of a suprasyndesmotic distal fibular fracture sustained during football practice, characterized by an unusual fracture mechanism without direct contact or major trauma and minimal clinical symptoms.

abstract.label: CASE REPORT
abstract.text: We present the case of a 15-year-old male admitted to the emergency department after an injury to the left leg while at a football practice. He reported missing the ball while attempting a shot and immediately perceived a crack in the kicking leg, without any collision or contact with another player. Clinical examination revealed painless palpation of both malleoli, varus stress testing, and isolated tenderness at the distal third of the fibula, without spontaneous pain.Radiographs confirmed a fracture located between the middle and distal thirds of the fibula, compatible with a suprasyndesmotic Weber C pattern.
