abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Severe asthma exacerbation incidence increased in the year before ICS initiation (13%-38%) and declined during the 1 to 3 years after initiation. In adjusted models, the odds of ≥ 1 severe asthma exacerbation decreased by 34% per year after initiation (adjusted OR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.59-0.74). ICS initiation was associated with lower recurrent exacerbation hazard in Andersen-Gill models and remained associated with reduced risk in marginal structural models. Greater reductions were observed among children with higher baseline asthma risk, whereas age at initiation did not significantly modify response.

abstract.label: INTERPRETATION
abstract.text: Our results show that ICS initiation was associated with significant attenuation of severe exacerbation burden in young children with asthma. These findings support early controller therapy in high-risk preschool populations while underscoring persistent heterogeneity and disparities in asthma outcomes.

articles.title: Extended-release guanfacine overdose in a pediatric emergency department: a systematic review and a 10-year retrospective chart review.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To characterize clinical presentations, management strategies and outcomes associated with extended-release guanfacine (ER guanfacine) overdose in pediatric patients presenting to a tertiary care pediatric emergency department (ED) supplemented with a systematic review of published pediatric cases.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective chart review included patients aged 0 to 18 years presenting with guanfacine overdose to a tertiary pediatric ED between August 2013 and July 2023. Data were extracted on demographics, cause of overdose, clinical features, management and outcomes. Concurrently, a systematic review using the population, exposure, and outcome approach searched MEDLINE and Embase (1974-November 2025) to consolidate existing case-report evidence on emergent management of guanfacine overdose in pediatric patients.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Ten studies met inclusion criteria, describing eleven pediatric cases, mostly accidental with ingestions in younger children, with bradycardia and hypotension reported frequently.Management was supportive; naloxone produced variable benefit, and when used no deaths occurred. For the retrospective cohort, (n = 15; median age 14), 73% involved intentional ingestions and were frequently associated with psychiatric comorbidities. Bradycardia and hypotension were nearly universal; with some patients demonstrating transient hypertension. Treatment included intravenous fluids (87%) and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia (20%). Three patients required pediatric intensive care unit admission; none received naloxone. All patients recovered fully without mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: ER guanfacine overdose most commonly affects adolescents with underlying mental health conditions and presents with clinically significant cardiovascular depression. Management is supportive, emphasizing fluid resuscitation and cardiac monitoring. Findings support the need for standardized ED care pathways and integrated mental-health interventions.

articles.title: Caught Between Care and Custody: Considerations for Carceral-Involved Youth in Emergency Departments and Inpatient Hospital Settings.

abstract.text: This article examines ethical, legal, and clinical challenges encountered when caring for carceral-involved youth in emergency and hospital settings. It highlights tensions between patient-centered care and law enforcement priorities, including issues of parental involvement, consent, privacy, autonomy, and the use of restraints. Law enforcement presence may compromise care through delays, coercion, and bias, disproportionately affecting minoritized populations. The authors emphasize that youth remain developmentally vulnerable patients requiring trauma-informed, family-centered care. They advocate for clear institutional policies, clinician education, and stronger pediatric-specific research to ensure dignity, protect rights, and mitigate harms at the intersection of health care and the carceral system.

articles.title: Analysis of Causes and Treatment of Facial Trauma in the Tulsa Metropolitan Area: A Level 2 Urban Trauma Center Experience.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Facial trauma remains a major public health issue, with causes that vary by region. National statistics often overlook local trends, which highlights the need for region-specific studies to create targeted prevention and treatment plans.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective review included 801 patients with facial fractures at a Level 2 urban trauma center, which serves the Tulsa metropolitan area with a population exceeding 1,000,000 residents. Data from patient records and the trauma registry between 2021 and 2024 were analyzed for demographics, injury mechanisms, fracture details, Injury Severity Score (ISS), comorbidities, treatments, and geographic origin (Tulsa versus other areas). χ2 tests examined categorical variables, while nonparametric tests evaluated continuous variables.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Most patients were male (73.8%) with an average age of 47.9 years. The main causes of injury were falls (23.4% overall; 51.0% in females versus 21.8% in males, P<0.001) and assaults (22.5% overall; 28.9% in males versus 13.8% in females, P<0.001). Firearm injuries were uncommon but more frequent among men (4.4% versus 0.5%, P<0.05). Falls made up 90.3% of injuries in patients over 85 years old (P<0.001). Major trauma (ISS >15) was seen in 25.6% of cases. Orbital floor fractures (16.1%) were more common than Le Fort fractures (8.4%). Comorbidities included substance use disorder (17.1%) and mental or psychiatric illnesses (12.2%). Patients from Tulsa had lower median ISS (9 versus 11, P=0.005) but higher rates of assault (31.9% versus 20.3%) and firearm injuries (5.0% versus 2.3%; P<0.05).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this urban Midwestern population, falls were more common in females and older adults, while intentional violence was higher among males and Tulsa residents. These findings underscore the need for tailored interventions: fall prevention for older adults and women, violence screening for men, and integrated approaches to substance use and mental health treatment.

articles.title: Comparing Disparate Application of Physical Restraints on Patients Seeking Emergency Mental Health Care at Two San Francisco Emergency Departments.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Black patients are more likely to receive physical restraints in both emergency department (ED) and inpatient settings, yet the mechanisms behind these disparities remain unclear. This study aims to assess whether hospital type-academic tertiary care center versus county-funded trauma hospital-drives the association between race and restraint use.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We used a community-based participatory research approach to analyze electronic medical record data from patients seen for a mental health emergency in 2019 and 2020 at two San Francisco hospitals, University of California, San Francisco Parnassus Hospital (UCSF) and Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital (ZSFG). Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests assessed patient characteristics by restraint, followed by multivariable logistic regression to estimate associations between race and restraint, stratified by hospital.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: We identified 6,631 unique encounters, with 1,051 (15.8%) involving physical restraints. At ZSFG ED, 19.2% of patients were restrained, and 12.6% at UCSF ED. In combined adjusted hospital analysis, Black patients had higher odds of restraint (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.16-2.05). Stratified analysis showed significantly higher odds of restraint for Black patients at UCSF ED (aOR 1.77, 95% CI 1.12-2.79), while ZSFG ED showed marginally higher odds of restraint for Black patients (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 0.99-2.09).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Our findings suggest that hospital type may not significantly influence disparate restraint use in EDs. Further research should explore other potential contributors, including prehospital interactions with emergency services.

abstract.label: HEALTH EQUITY IMPLICATIONS
abstract.text: These results highlight the need for interventions that address the broader impact of structural racism on patients in mental health crises.

articles.title: Nurses' Experiences Caring for Hospitalized Patients With Opioid Use Disorders.

abstract.text: The purpose of this study was to examine nurses' experience of care for hospitalized patients with a history of opioid use disorder (OUD). A national sample of 179 nurses completed an online survey regarding their experiences on caring for patients with OUD. Most participants were staff nurses who worked in emergency departments, critical care units, or perinatal units. Only 41.9% of the participants received education regarding OUD from their employers, and even fewer nurses had participated in harm reduction education. Less than half (45.0%) of the nurses had knowledge regarding harm reduction strategies. Most participants experienced a low number of restrictive safety measures designed to protect patients, adverse events associated with care of their patients with OUD, and effective care interventions when caring for patients with OUD. Almost all the nurses (97.5%) experienced a patient with an OUD leave the hospital against hospital advice (or direct their own discharge). Most nurses rated quality care and their own satisfaction when caring for patients with an OUD as average. Content analysis of open-ended questions regarding equity and patient-centeredness of care supported quantitative findings. The study findings contribute to current evidence regarding the need for standardized hospital policies aimed at improving quality care, and hospitals should incorporate harm reduction strategies in training and practices that are patient-centered and evidence-based.

articles.title: Enhancing Educational Programs and Communication Strategies to Address Alcohol Use Among EMS Providers.

abstract.text: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers experience substantial occupational stress, which may contribute to alcohol use as a coping mechanism. Despite growing attention to workforce wellness among first responders, relatively little research has examined how alcohol-related education should be developed and delivered for EMS providers. This qualitative study explored non-fire-based EMS providers' perspectives on alcohol-related education, training, and support through semi-structured interviews with 31 EMS clinicians representing multiple certification levels and regions of the United States. Participants consistently described existing alcohol-related education as limited, passive, and focused primarily on patient care rather than provider well-being. They recommended educational approaches that incorporate EMS-specific data, information on the physiological effects of alcohol, personal narratives, and interactive instructional strategies. Participants also emphasized the importance of broader support systems, including peer support, family involvement, and improved awareness of available resources. Taken together, these findings suggest that alcohol-related education in EMS should be tailored to the occupational realities of the profession and integrated with broader efforts to support workforce health and well-being.

articles.title: Incidence of Electrolyte Abnormalities in Emergency Department Patients Presenting With Ethanol Intoxication.
articles.journal_full: WMJ : official publication of the State Medical Society of Wisconsin

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Ethanol intoxication is the most common substance use-related emergency department (ED) presentation in the United States, and the proportion of ethanol-related ED visits is increasing. Although ethanol ingestion can lead to electrolyte abnormalities, ethanol intoxication is often diagnosed on the basis of physical examination, and clinicians frequently defer laboratory testing in clinically intoxicated patients. The purpose of this study was to describe the incidence of electrolyte abnormalities in a cohort of patients evaluated in the ED for ethanol intoxication.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective cohort study was performed on Veteran Affairs (VA) ED visit data from 2010 through 2019. Eligible encounters included ED visits with a serum ethanol concentration greater than 50 mg/dL and available electrolyte results.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 223456 encounters involving 83178 patients were included in the analysis. The study population was 94.2% male, and the median age was 55 years. Overall, 48.8% of encounters had at least 1 electrolyte abnormality, and 2.9% had a severe electrolyte abnormality. Hypokalemia was associated with hypomagnesemia (OR, 2.64; 95% CI, 2.56-2.73) and hypophosphatemia (OR, 2.51; 95% CI, 2.21-2.84).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The prevalence of electrolyte derangements was substantial among patients with ethanol intoxication. Abnormalities in commonly measured electrolytes were associated with abnormalities in less frequently measured electrolytes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Routine serum chemistry testing should be considered in patients presenting with ethanol-related complaints to screen for electrolyte abnormalities. In particular, hypokalemia should increase concern for hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia.

articles.title: Wrong-Way Driving and Injury Risk on a Rural Four-Lane Corridor: A Descriptive and Spatial Analysis of US Highway 10, 2019-2024.
articles.journal_full: WMJ : official publication of the State Medical Society of Wisconsin

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) on rural highways pose unique challenges due to high speed limits, limited access points, and varied environmental conditions. This study aimed to describe crash characteristics, identify predictors of injury and fatality, and evaluate geospatial trends along a rural segment of US Highway 10 in Wisconsin.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective analysis of MVCs reported on US Highway 10 from January 1, 2019, to March 1, 2024. Incident-level dispatch data were analyzed with corresponding environmental and temporal factors using descriptive statistics, geospatial analysis, and logistic regression. Geospatial mapping was used to identify high-risk roadway segments, and descriptive statistics and logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with injury or fatality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 239 MVCs, 21.3% (n = 51) involved injury or death. Angle collisions were significantly associated with increased odds of injury or fatality (OR 2.52; 95% CI, 1.04-6.09, P = .04). Wrong-way driving, though rare, was associated with a higher proportion of injury-producing crashes. Deer-related crashes comprised 38.0% of events but rarely resulted in injury (4.3%). Environmental factors, including lighting conditions, road surface conditions, and weather, were not independently predictive. Spatial clustering was observed near major intersections, transition zones, and roadway merging areas.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Collision mechanism, particularly angle collisions and wrong-way crashes, are key predictors of injury on this rural 4-lane highway corridor. In contrast, deer-related collisions were common but infrequently associated with injury. These findings support targeted roadway-engineering improvement, enhanced signage, and behavioral interventions to reduce crash-related injury along rural corridors such as Highway 10.

articles.title: One Size Does Not Fit All: Is Whole-body Computed Tomography Beneficial for All Patients with Suspected Major Trauma? A Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) is increasingly used for major trauma, but its clinical benefits must be balanced against radiation exposure and resource utilization. This study aimed to explore the clinical benefits and radiation-related risks of WBCT across distinct trauma activation subgroups and to evaluate whether imaging strategies should be tailored to individual patient characteristics.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted this prospective randomized controlled trial at a Level I trauma center between March 2010 and January 2012. Patients meeting predefined trauma-team activation criteria were randomized to WBCT or conventional imaging. We evaluated diagnostic workflow, mortality, radiation exposure, complications, and delayed diagnoses. Patients were further classified into hemodynamically unstable, altered mental status, and mechanism-only activation subgroups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 151 patients were included in the final analysis: 73 in the WBCT group and 78 in the conventional group. WBCT required longer primary imaging time than conventional imaging (36 [IQR 30-47] vs. 31 [IQR 24-39] minutes, p = 0.002), but final decision-making time showed a non-significant trend toward reduction (96 vs. 128.5 minutes, p = 0.142). No statistically significant differences were observed in mortality, complications, or delayed diagnoses. Delayed diagnoses occurred in 18/73 patients (24.7%) in the WBCT group and 11/78 patients (14.1%) in the conventional group (p = 0.100). In subgroup analyses, WBCT was associated with lower radiation exposure among unstable patients (23.9 vs. 35.4 mSv, p = 0.02) but higher exposure among unconscious patients (24.9 vs. 18.0 mSv, p = 0.01). Because the final sample was substantially smaller than planned, the study was underpowered to detect differences in relatively infrequent clinical outcomes, particularly mortality and delayed diagnosis.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: The potential value of WBCT may depend on the clinical scenario and the diagnostic pathway used. In our study, the differences in radiation exposure among trauma activation subgroups suggest that the trade-off between comprehensive imaging and radiation burden may not be uniform across patients. In addition, comprehensive imaging cannot replace repeated clinical assessment and tertiary evaluation for detecting subtle or delayed injuries.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In this underpowered randomized cohort, WBCT did not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in survival or delayed diagnosis. Its potential benefits appeared to vary according to clinical presentation, suggesting that WBCT should be selectively tailored to individual patient characteristics and trauma-system context.

abstract.label: TRIAL REGISTRATION
abstract.text: Current Controlled Trials ISRCTN32471051, retrospectively registered on November 05, 2025.

articles.title: Point of Care (POCUS) Gastric Ultrasound to Predict Gastric Volume in Patients Presenting for Emergency Surgeries.

abstract.text: Background In emergency surgery, pulmonary aspiration is a significant anesthetic risk. Traditional fasting hours are often unreliable due to physiological stress. This study evaluated the utility of point-of-care gastric ultrasound in assessing gastric volume and content in an emergency Nepalese cohort. Objective To determine the volume, content and cross sectional area of gastric antrum in emergency surgeries and to determine if they are correlated with age, fasting hours, comorbidity, pain score, body mass index and opioid. Method A prospective cross-sectional study of 145 adult patients was conducted. Gastric antral cross-sectional area was measured in the right lateral decubitus position. Gastric volume was calculated using validated formula. Gastric content was noted. These were correlated with variables using univariate and multivariate regression. Result The mean fasting time was 11.05 ± 4.20 hours. However, gastric ultrasound revealed that 42.7% of patients had gastric contents (37.9% clear fluid, 4.8% solids). Furthermore, 21.4% of patients exceeded the high-risk volume threshold of 1.5 mL/ kg. In the multivariate analysis, advanced age (p = 0.003) and higher visual analogue scale score (p =0.03) were independent predictors of gastric volume and gastric cross sectional area. Conclusion Fasting hours are a poor surrogate for gastric emptiness in emergency settings. One in five patients meeting nil per oral criteria remained at high risk for aspiration. We recommend the routine use of preoperative gastric ultrasound, especially in older patients and those with high pain scores, to individualize airway management.
